questions.question: Evaluate protein digestion and assess the role of brush-border peptidases in the final stages of protein digestion.
questions.solution_html:
• of protein digestion.
  • Protein digestion is the process by which dietary proteins are broken down into
  • amino acids so that they can be absorbed and used by the body. This process
  • begins in the stomach, where the acidic environment (hydrochloric acid)
  • denatures proteins and activates the enzyme pepsin from its inactive form
  • pepsinogen. Pepsin breaks proteins into smaller polypeptides.
  • In the small intestine, protein digestion continues with the help of pancreatic enzymes
  • such as trypsin, chymotrypsin, elastase, and carboxypeptidases, which further break
  • polypeptides into smaller peptides and amino acids.
  • intestinal peptidases present on the brush border of intestinal cells convert peptides
  • into free amino acids, dipeptides, and tripeptides.
questions.final_answer: into free amino acids, dipeptides, and tripeptides

questions.question: Explain and illustrate why urine turns dark on standing in alkaptonuria.
questions.solution_html:
• Alkaptonuria is a rare inborn error of metabolism caused by a deficiency of the
  • enzyme homogentisic acid oxidase, which is involved in the metabolism of the
  • amino acids phenylalanine and tyrosine. Due to this enzyme defect
  • homogentisic acid accumulates in the body and is excreted in the urine.
  • A characteristic feature of alkaptonuria is that the urine turns dark brown or black on
  • standing due to oxidation of homogentisic acid.
questions.final_answer: standing due to oxidation of homogentisic acid
questions.source_exam: MGU-UGP (HONOURS) 2024 Admission Regular Exam Sem 4, March 2026

questions.question: Why is α-oxidation necessary in fatty acid metabolism?
questions.solution_html:
• α-Oxidation occurs in the peroxisomes and is important for the oxidation of
  • branched-chain fatty acids, such as phytanic acid. It involves the removal of
  • one carbon atom at a time and is necessary because branched fatty acids
  • cannot undergo normal β-oxidation directly.

questions.question: Describe how transamination reactions contribute to the formation of glutamate.
questions.solution_html:
• Transaminations are freely reversible reactions catalyzed by transaminases
  • (aminotransferases). Amino group of α-amino acid is exchanged with oxo
  • group of 2-oxoacidduring transamination. The amino group is transferred by
  • cofactor pyridoxal phosphate (PLP, derivative of vitamin B6) to oxoacid.Most
  • of the amino acids undergo transamination in their degradation. Enzymes
  • aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) are
  • examples of transaminases that are normally detected as markers of potential
  • damage to the liver cells.
